instruction: Describe a time when you used information for tourists, for example from a guidebook or online.
response: I'd like to talk about a trip to Xi'an a couple of years ago, where I depended almost entirely on online tourist information rather than a guidebook, and it completely changed how I travel. Before the trip, I'd done my usual research — the obvious sites, the Terracotta Warriors, the City Wall — but the real discovery came from travel forums and a few local blogs written by people who actually lived there. One post in particular warned me that the Warriors' main pit is mobbed by mid-morning and recommended arriving right at opening time and seeing Pit One last, once the tour groups had cycled through. Honestly, I was sceptical — travel advice always sounds more clever than it is — but I followed it, and it worked spectacularly. At eight in the morning I stood nearly alone in front of the army, and the silence made the whole thing feel almost sacred. The same blog pointed me to a tiny family-run restaurant serving biangbiang noodles down an alley I would never have entered otherwise, and to a section of the old wall you could cycle at sunset, when the light turns everything gold. What struck me afterwards was how different the trip felt from my earlier holidays, which were essentially checklist tours built from guidebooks. This time, the information came with opinions and personality — someone telling me what they loved and what they'd skip — and that made all the difference. Was it helpful? Enormously. It saved me hours of queuing, introduced me to food I now cook at home, and taught me a lasting lesson: guidebooks tell you what a place is famous for, but locals tell you what a place is actually like.

instruction: Describe a time when you read or heard something that you thought was not true.
response: I'd like to describe a time I read something online that I instinctively knew wasn't true — a viral post about a supposed change to the national pension age that was going to 'take effect next month'. I came across it late one evening, forwarded by a relative in our family group chat with a wall of exclamation marks, and it spread through the group like wildfire. My suspicion was triggered almost immediately, and for three specific reasons. First, the post cited no official source whatsoever — no ministry name, no document number, nothing you could actually verify. Second, the writing had all the fingerprints of manufactured outrage: urgent capital letters, phrases like 'they don't want you to know', and a demand to forward it to everyone you care about. Genuine announcements read like announcements; this read like bait. Third, and most tellingly, I checked the official government website and the major news portals, and there was absolutely nothing there — a real policy change of that scale would be everywhere. So I replied with a link to the official channel and a gentle suggestion to double-check before forwarding, and, to their credit, my relatives stood down. Interestingly, the original post had already been flagged and debunked by a fact-checking site, which confirmed what my instincts had told me within about thirty seconds. The whole episode left me with a lasting takeaway: emotional urgency is precisely the product being sold in these posts, and calm scepticism costs nothing. These days my family's group chat has an unofficial rule — check before you share — which, honestly, feels like real progress.

instruction: Describe an interesting garden or park you have seen.
response: The garden I'd like to describe is the Humble Administrator's Garden in Suzhou, which I visited a few years ago and which genuinely redefined what I thought a garden could be. It's a classical Chinese garden dating back to the Ming Dynasty — over five hundred years old — and it's recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage site, though frankly no title is needed to see that something special is going on there. What makes it interesting is that it isn't really about flowers at all; it's a piece of philosophy built in stone and water. The garden is designed so that every view is composed like a painting: a zigzag bridge that forces you to slow down, pavilions positioned so you glimpse the pond through a round 'moon gate', and rocks carefully arranged to resemble miniature mountains. Our guide explained that the designers deliberately used framing and hidden pathways so the garden feels far larger than its actual size — you keep turning corners and discovering new scenes, like chapters in a book. The pond is the heart of everything: koi drifting beneath willow branches, and on the water's surface the reflections of the pavilions, which are, in a sense, just as real as the buildings themselves. I visited in late spring, with the wisteria in bloom, and the whole place smelled faintly green and ancient. What stayed with me most was the intentionality behind it all — nothing was accidental. Every stone had been chosen; every window had been shaped to crop a particular view. Modern parks give you space; this garden gave me the strange, humbling realisation that a handful of acres can contain an entire worldview, and that people half a millennium ago understood landscape design better than we usually give them credit for.

instruction: Describe a person you know who is very competitive.
response: The most competitive person I know is my university friend Kevin, and I mean that with genuine affection — mostly. We met on the badminton court, which is fitting, because Kevin treats every badminton rally like a world championship final. What makes him unusual isn't just that he wants to win; everyone says that. It's the thoroughness of it. He studied our playing styles the way a coach would — he knew I always favoured my backhand under pressure, and he'd aim there relentlessly, then look delighted about it. And it's absolutely not limited to sport. Board games, office trivia, even guessing the bill total first at dinner — Kevin converts every moment into a contest, usually with a running scoreboard he maintains in his head. He once trained for a month before our department's table tennis tournament, and when he won, he was gracious for exactly four seconds before mentioning that he'd 'predicted the whole bracket'. Why is he like this? I've asked him, half-jokingly, many times. His answer is that competition is how he shows he cares — he gives you his full effort because offering anything less would be disrespectful. There's something oddly touching about that framing. The flip side is real, of course: he sulks magnificently when he loses, and cooperative tasks sometimes become solo missions because he'd rather do everything himself than trust someone to match his standard. But I'll say this for him — being around Kevin raises your own game. I've never trained harder, laughed louder, or lost more graciously than I have against him, and losing to Kevin is at least a learning experience, usually delivered with commentary.

topic: a play or film to see again
instruction: Describe a play or a film you have seen that you would like to see again with friends.
response: The film I'd love to rewatch with friends is 'The Truman Show', which I first saw at university during a film club screening — and which completely hijacked my thoughts for a week afterwards. For those who haven't seen it, it's about a man named Truman whose entire life is, unknown to him, a television show: everyone in his hometown is an actor, every conversation is scripted, and millions of people watch his ordinary days as entertainment. On the surface it's a comedy, and it is genuinely funny — Jim Carrey is wonderful in it. But the reason I want to see it again with friends is the layers underneath. The first time, I watched it as a story about a trapped man. The second time, I realised it was really about me — about how much of my own life runs on autopilot, following routines I never chose to question. That's the kind of film that changes depending on who you are when you watch it. I'd particularly love to watch it with my close friends because we'd talk for hours afterwards, and that post-film conversation is honestly half the experience. One friend is obsessed with media ethics, so he'd take the television company's perspective apart. Another works in advertising and would notice every fake product placement. And we'd inevitably end up debating the ending — whether Truman's final line and that deliberate little bow are triumphant or heartbreaking. I've seen it twice, and both times it felt like a different film. Some films you watch once and file away; this one feels like a conversation you want to keep having, just with different people in the room. That's why, if I could pick any film for our next gathering, it would be this one — preferably followed by a long dinner.

instruction: Describe a time when you changed a plan you had made.
response: I'd like to talk about a trip I replanned entirely at the last minute — a holiday that was supposed to be in Japan but ended up being a train journey through southern China. I'd been preparing the Japan trip for months: flights booked, a carefully colour-coded itinerary, restaurant reservations, the lot. Then, about ten days before departure, a typhoon warning was issued for exactly the week I was due to travel. My first instinct was to wait it out, but the forecasts kept worsening, and the airline began offering full refunds. So, one Thursday evening, I made the decision that felt almost physically painful: I cancelled everything. The strange part is what happened next. Sitting there with a refund and a suddenly empty week, I opened a map and asked myself where I'd actually wanted to go for years but never had the excuse — and the answer was the old towns of southern China. I booked a train that night with zero planning beyond the first ticket, and honestly, that trip became one of the best I've ever taken. Without an itinerary, I said yes to everything: a detour to a mountain village recommended by a fellow passenger, three days in a small town eating food I couldn't name, an extra night somewhere simply because the rain made it pretty. The original plan would have produced a good holiday; this one produced stories. What did I feel about changing it? At the moment of cancellation — genuinely upset; I'd invested so much in those spreadsheets. In hindsight — grateful, and permanently changed. I still plan trips, but far more loosely now. My philosophy has become: plan the direction, leave the rest to luck and curiosity.

topic: a piece of work you were satisfied with
instruction: Describe a piece of work you did for your job or your studies that you felt very satisfied with.
response: I'd like to describe a teaching project from a couple of years ago that remains my proudest piece of professional work. I was given a class of students who'd failed the IELTS speaking section multiple times, and honestly, they'd given up on themselves — they walked in with that particular defeated posture of people expecting to fail again. The standard course materials weren't working for them; the exercises assumed confidence they simply didn't have. So, with my manager's reluctant blessing, I threw out the textbook for that class and built a new programme from scratch. The core idea was simple: make speaking small and safe before making it big. We started with ninety-second recordings — just answering one question into a phone, alone, where nobody could judge them. Then we gradually built up: pair practice, small groups, then full mock tests, with every stage recorded so they could literally hear themselves improving week by week. That last part was the secret weapon. Students who claimed they'd 'never improve' listened to their week-one recordings in week ten and were visibly shocked. The course finished with a full mock exam in front of unfamiliar examiners — terrifying by design — and their results when the real test came were beyond anything the class had achieved before: nearly everyone cleared the score they needed, and one student, who'd failed four times previously, scored higher than students in my advanced class. Why was I so satisfied? Partly the results, yes, but mostly the transformation — watching people who'd decided they were 'just bad at speaking' rediscover their own voice. Materials get replaced, but that feeling doesn't expire. It's the benchmark I measure every class against now, and honestly, few things since have matched it.

topic: a long discussion about a news story
instruction: Describe a time when you had a long discussion about a news story.
response: I'd like to describe a discussion that started over lunch and somehow swallowed an entire afternoon — about the news that a major city had announced plans to ban private cars from its historic centre entirely. I'd read the article that morning, and when a colleague mentioned it, we started comparing reactions. He was against it immediately: delivery businesses, elderly residents, emergency access — he listed practical objections faster than I could drink my soup. I was more sympathetic to the idea, having lived through years of exhaust fumes and honking, so naturally I defended the other side. What made the discussion long wasn't stubbornness, though; it was that each argument genuinely opened a new question. When he raised deliveries, we got into how cities could use cargo bikes and night-time consolidation — he countered with cost, I countered with subsidies, and suddenly we were debating whether city centres should be shaped by economics or quality of life. Then a second colleague joined and reframed everything around her grandmother, who can't walk far and depends on her car — and that silenced both of us for a moment, in a useful way. We eventually drifted into comparing cities we'd visited: which ones felt alive, which felt like car parks with shops attached, and why the differences weren't really about cars at all but about whether streets were designed for people or for vehicles. By the time we looked up, the café had emptied and the afternoon had gone. What I remember most is the quality of the disagreement — nobody was performing for an audience, nobody was trying to win, and we all shifted position at least once. It's the rare kind of conversation where you leave having genuinely changed how you see something, and I'd happily lose another afternoon to it.

instruction: Describe a law that was introduced in your country and that you thought was a very good idea.
response: The law I'd like to talk about is the nationwide smoking ban in indoor public places, which I genuinely consider one of the best pieces of legislation in my lifetime. It was introduced in stages — first restaurants and bars in the big cities, then workplaces, public transport and eventually indoor spaces across the country — and I remember the rollout clearly because I was at university when it happened. Before the ban, going to a restaurant was a strange ordeal: you'd request the non-smoking section, which was a purely theoretical concept, usually one table placed directly next to the smoking section, so you breathed the same air with extra steps. And long-distance train journeys were honestly grim; fifteen hours in a carriage where smoking was tolerated was an experience you endured rather than enjoyed. The change after the ban was immediate and, looking back, astonishing in how quickly it became normal. Within a year, seeing someone smoke indoors produced genuine shock — the social norm had flipped completely, and it flipped because the law gave non-smokers the backing they'd never had. What I think makes it such a good law, though, goes beyond the obvious health benefits, real as those are — fewer heart attacks, cleaner air, children not breathing smoke with their dinner. It's that it changed behaviour without needing constant enforcement. Most people comply not because they fear a fine but because the new norm feels natural now, which is the mark of legislation done well: it doesn't just punish, it persuades. My father, who smoked for thirty years, actually credits the ban with helping him quit — he said it was easier to stop when the world stopped cooperating with the habit. A law that quietly improves health, protects people who can't protect themselves, and even changes individual lives — that's about as good as laws get.

topic: a person who won a prize
instruction: Describe a person from your country who has won a prize, award or medal.
response: The person I'd like to talk about is Tu Youyou, who won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2015 — the first Chinese scientist to win a Nobel in that category, and a figure I find quietly extraordinary. She received it for discovering artemisinin, the drug that became the world's most effective treatment for malaria. What makes her story remarkable is how it happened. In the late 1960s, she was appointed to a secret military project to find a cure for malaria, which was devastating soldiers and civilians across Southeast Asia. The team screened hundreds of traditional herbs with little success, until Tu went back to ancient medical texts and found a reference to sweet wormwood — but with a crucial detail: the extraction method in the text suggested a cold process. Following that hint, she realised that heat was destroying the active compound, changed the extraction technique, and produced the compound that would go on to save millions of lives. There's a detail from her story that I find genuinely humbling: to test the drug's safety before clinical trials, she and colleagues volunteered to take it themselves. And when she won the Nobel — after decades of working in relative obscurity, without a doctorate, without overseas training, without membership in the big academies — she accepted it with characteristic modesty, calling the prize an honour for her whole team and for traditional Chinese medicine. Was it right that she received it? Absolutely, and arguably overdue. In an era when science is often noisy, self-promotional and celebrity-driven, her career was the opposite: decades of patient, methodical work driven by a single question. She's proof that the most important discoveries don't announce themselves — they just quietly save millions of lives.

instruction: Describe a car journey you made that took longer than expected.
response: I'd like to describe a car journey that was supposed to take four hours and ended up taking eleven — a family trip to my uncle's place in the countryside during the Spring Festival travel rush. We'd planned it carefully, which is what makes the story funnier in hindsight: early start, route checked, snacks packed. My father even said, famously, 'We'll be there by lunch.' The first sign of trouble came an hour in, when the highway app turned deep red — an accident had closed two lanes, and every alternative route was absorbing the overflow. We crawled. Then came the snow, which nobody had forecast properly, and the highway authorities closed a mountain tunnel section for safety, rerouting everyone onto country roads designed, I can only assume, for horse carts. At one point we were stationary so long that my mother produced boiled eggs from her bottomless bag, and we had a full lunch in the car, parked, on a rural road, between fields. And here's the thing I want to explain: it should have been miserable, and by any rational measure it was — but it turned out to be one of the warmest family days I can remember. Cut off from screens and schedules, we talked. Properly talked. My father told stories about his childhood I'd never heard; my sister and I played those endless word games from our childhood; we sang badly. When we finally rolled in at eleven at night, my uncle was waiting with hot food and, to his eternal credit, no questions asked. What did I take from it? Mostly that a journey's quality isn't measured in hours. The delay was out of our control, but the mood was ours to choose, and we chose well. These days, whenever traffic grounds us to a halt, my family just looks at each other and says: boiled eggs?

instruction: Describe a place you visited that has beautiful views.
response: The place I'd like to describe is Yangshuo, in Guangxi, which I visited with two friends during a university holiday, and which I still consider the most visually stunning place I've ever stood in. Yangshuo sits in the middle of the famous karst landscape — those extraordinary limestone towers that rise straight out of the ground like the backs of sleeping dragons. Photos don't prepare you for them. In photographs they look like a backdrop; in person they surround you completely, layered into the mist at different distances, and your sense of scale simply gives up. We spent three days there, and each one offered a different way of seeing the same jaw-dropping scenery. The first was from the water: we took a bamboo raft down the Yulong River, drifting past water buffalo and fishermen with cormorants, the peaks sliding by on both banks. That's the slow version, and it's the best one. The second was from above — we climbed Xianggong Hill before dawn, which involved a genuinely undignified scramble in the dark, and watched the sunrise pour gold over a valley of mist with karst islands floating in it like a classical ink painting. Nobody spoke for about ten minutes. The third was the humbler version: cycling between villages, past rice paddies and orange trees, with the peaks following us everywhere like patient escorts. What made the views beautiful to me wasn't just the geology — it was the layering: mist, water, green fields, grey stone, all constantly rearranging with the light. I've been to famous viewpoints in several countries, but Yangshuo is the only place I've returned to in my imagination repeatedly. It's the standard against which I now measure every sunset, which is frankly unfair to all other sunsets.

topic: learning to prepare food or drink
instruction: Describe some food or drink that you learned to prepare.
response: I'd like to talk about learning to make dumplings properly, which sounds humble but which took me an embarrassingly long time to master. The setting was my grandmother's kitchen during a winter holiday, back when I was at university. Dumplings had always appeared on our table as if by magic — my grandmother produced them at a speed I assumed was genetic. That year, instead of letting me do my usual job of eating, she put the rolling pin in my hand. The first lesson was humility. My wrappers came out either elephant-thick or full of holes, and my first attempts at folding produced objects that looked less like dumplings and more like small defeated envelopes — several of which burst dramatically in the pot, releasing their filling into what became, essentially, soup. My grandmother watched all this with the serene patience of someone who has taught forty years of clumsy grandchildren, and kept repeating the two secrets: the dough has to rest, and you have to trust the pleat. She didn't demonstrate faster; she slowed everything down and made me feel each step — how the wrapper should be thinner at the edges, how much filling is exactly enough, how the final squeeze is a promise the dough keeps if you've done everything else right. By the third afternoon, something clicked. My dumplings started looking like dumplings, and more importantly, they stayed sealed in the pot. The first batch my family actually ate and complimented — rather than politely rescued — is a small moment I still treasure. What I learned went beyond the recipe, though. Dumpling-making is really about assembly lines and conversation: someone rolls, someone fills, everyone talks, and the food is almost a by-product of the company. Now, whenever I make dumplings with friends, I use my grandmother's phrases, and I like to think the technique — and the patience — is quietly being passed down.

instruction: Describe a tourist attraction in your country that you would recommend.
response: The attraction I'd recommend is the ancient town of Pingyao, in Shanxi province, which I visited a few years ago and which remains my favourite answer when foreign friends ask what to see beyond Beijing. Pingyao is a remarkably complete walled city from the Ming and Qing dynasties — one of the very few in China whose original city wall, streets, courtyards and even banks have survived largely intact. It's a UNESCO World Heritage site, but the statistics undersell the experience of actually walking it. What makes it special is the coherence. In most ancient towns, you get a restored 'old street' surrounded by modern sprawl; Pingyao is the whole thing — four kilometres of original city wall you can walk on top of, watchtowers, temples, and narrow lanes where people genuinely live. It's like stepping into a historical photograph that somehow has running water and excellent noodles. Two things in particular stuck with me. The first is Rishengchang, considered China's first draft bank, founded in the Qing dynasty — standing in its dim courtyards, you realise this small northern town was once the financial heart of the empire, with branches as far away as Japan and Russia. The second is simply the evening atmosphere: as tour buses leave, lanterns come on, locals settle into doorways, and the town belongs to wanderers again. My practical advice to visitors is to stay overnight inside the walls — day-trippers only see half of it — and to go in autumn, when the light is soft and the crowds thin. I recommend Pingyao over flashier destinations because it offers something increasingly rare: depth without performance. It isn't a theme park version of history; it's the real thing, slightly worn, still breathing, and all the more moving for it.

topic: visiting a family member at home
instruction: Describe a time when you enjoyed visiting a member of your family in their home.
response: I'd like to describe a visit to my aunt's home in the countryside two springs ago, which I still count as one of my favourite weekends in recent memory. My aunt moved out of the city after retiring, to a small house with a vegetable garden and an orchard, and she'd been inviting me for ages. Work kept getting in the way until finally I blocked out a long weekend and took the slow train out — which, incidentally, was the right choice, because the last hour winds through orchards in blossom. What made the visit special was the rhythm of her life, which was completely alien to mine and utterly restorative. Days there have a shape: up early with the birds, tea in the courtyard, then the vegetable garden, where I was immediately put to work and immediately criticised — apparently there is a correct way to pull weeds, and I was not doing it. There were also, for the record, chickens, and one of them held a personal grudge against me for reasons that were never fully explained. We cooked together — everything from the garden, nothing bought except salt — and I was taught her dumpling wrapping technique, which differs from my grandmother's and which I was sworn to keep secret. Evenings were the best part: dinner in the yard as the light went down, my uncle telling stories, fireflies doing their small silent show over the garden wall. No screens, no schedule, and the deepest sleep I've had in years. What I enjoyed most, I think, was being useful in a simple way — hands in the soil, helping with something real — and being looked after without any of the usual noise of modern life. I've been back twice since, and I now understand why she never wants to move back to the city.

topic: meeting someone who became a good friend
instruction: Describe a time when you met someone who you became good friends with.
response: I'd like to talk about how I met my friend David, in circumstances so mundane that our friendship feels like a small statistical miracle. It was about four years ago, at a badminton court near my flat. I'd turned up to a casual session organised online, where strangers book a court and hope enough people appear. That evening, exactly two of us showed up — me and David — which could have been an awkward hour of polite rallies. Instead, we ended up playing for two and a half hours. My first impression of him was that he was quietly competitive in the best way — he pushed hard, laughed at his own mistakes, and had an evident policy of never letting a point die without effort. Between games we got talking, and I discovered he'd also recently moved to the city, also didn't know anyone, and also had that specific look of someone surviving on work colleagues alone. That shared situation did half the work; the other half was that he was simply easy to talk to — curious without prying, funny without performing. Afterwards he said, 'Same time next week?', and it became a standing arrangement before either of us formally decided it. From badminton we graduated to dinners, then to being each other's default plus-one for everything. What cemented it, though, was a bad patch: when I was dealing with a family illness a year later, David was the one who showed up with food, handled practical things without being asked, and never once made me feel like a burden. That's when friendship quietly upgraded from habit to loyalty. We still play every week. Our badminton has improved only marginally, but the friendship that accidentally started on that nearly-empty court has become one of the most dependable things in my life — all because two strangers showed up.

instruction: Describe the neighbourhood you lived in when you were a child.
response: I'd like to describe the neighbourhood where I grew up — a dense, lively block of old low-rise housing that I lived in until I was about twelve, before we moved to a newer district. Physically, it was nothing special: narrow lanes too tight for cars, laundry strung between balconies, and walls thin enough that you knew your neighbours' TV schedules by heart. But that was precisely its magic. In that neighbourhood, privacy was a rumour and community was a fact. My mother could send me to the corner shop with a note and the shopkeeper would add her credit to a worn notebook — actual credit, tracked in pencil, based purely on trust. Dinner was a rolling event: whatever anyone cooked too much of travelled between kitchens, so most nights I ate from three or four households. The children were one big pack, governed by age and led by whoever owned the best football; we turned the lane into a stadium every evening until a parent's shout brought the match to its inevitable abandoned conclusion. There was an old bicycle repairman at the entrance whose shed served as the unofficial town hall, where disputes were settled and the day's news was analysed. Was it perfect? No — it was noisy, cramped, and when it rained hard, certain lanes turned into shallow rivers. I didn't appreciate any of it at the time; I thought wealthier districts with their lifts and their big windows were obviously better. Now I understand what we had: a childhood spent outdoors, supervised by an entire street of surrogate aunts and uncles who all felt entitled to tell me off. When I went back recently, most of it was gone — redeveloped, as such places always are. But walking those remaining lanes, I felt something the new flat never managed to give me: the sense of belonging to a place that also belonged to me.

instruction: Describe a big city you would like to visit.
response: The big city I'd most like to visit is Chengdu, in southwest China, and my reasons are honestly a little embarrassing in how food-centred they are. Chengdu is, of course, a massive modern metropolis — twenty million people, skyscrapers, the works — but its global reputation rests on two pillars: the panda breeding base on its outskirts, and a food culture so passionate that UNESCO named it a City of Gastronomy, the first in Asia. Let me start with the pandas, because how could I not. The Chengdu Research Base is the world's leading centre for breeding giant pandas, and visitors can watch them at unnervingly close range — including, if you time it right, the baby pandas, which are reportedly nature's most efficient generators of joy. I'd go at opening time, because pandas do everything important before ten a.m. and then, quite reasonably, sleep for the rest of the day — an approach to life I find deeply relatable. But the city itself is the bigger draw for me. Chengdu's food is legendary: hotpot that locals eat even in humid summers, mapo tofu from its birthplace, and street snacks on every corner. There's a saying that visitors to Chengdu never want to leave, and I'd like to test it personally. Beyond eating, I'm drawn to the city's famous pace. Chinese cities have reputations for rushing, but Chengdu is the celebrated exception — teahouses full of people playing mahjong for entire afternoons, opera houses performing the ancient art of face-changing, and a general air that life is for enjoying. I'd travel there by high-speed rail, deliberately, because the journey through the mountains is part of the experience. In a trip I'd split my time: mornings at the base and the temples, afternoons in teahouses watching the world stroll by, and every single evening eating something that hurts slightly. That, to me, is a perfect city break.

instruction: Describe a monument (e.g., a statue or sculpture) that you like.
response: The monument I'd like to describe is the Leshan Giant Buddha, a colossal stone statue carved into a riverside cliff in Sichuan province, which I visited several years ago and which left me genuinely speechless. First, the sheer facts, because they deserve to be said slowly: the Buddha is seventy-one metres tall, carved directly out of the cliff face, and construction began in the year 713. It took roughly ninety years to complete. People laboured on this across multiple generations — most of them never lived to see it finished. The reason it was built is the part I find most moving. A monk named Haitong began the project because the confluence of three rivers below the cliff was treacherous, and boats were constantly wrecking; he believed a Buddha's presence would calm the turbulent waters. In a beautiful twist that feels almost fictional, the rubble from the carving was dumped into the river and actually did alter the current, making the crossing safer. The engineering, in other words, accidentally fulfilled the prayer. Standing at the Buddha's feet — and the feet alone are larger than most rooms — I had the sensation I've only had a few times in my life: the complete failure of scale. You look up and your neck gives up before your comprehension does. The detail is what gets you: the 1,021 spiral coils of hair, each one bigger than a person; the drainage system hidden inside the statue, carved a thousand years ago, still protecting it from rain erosion today. What I like most about the monument, though, is what it represents: not power, not conquest, but a monk's stubborn compassion turned into stone across nine decades. Monuments usually commemorate people; this one commemorates care itself. It's the most human thing I've ever seen made of rock.

instruction: Describe an occasion when you had to do something in a hurry.
response: I'd like to describe the morning I nearly missed a flight to Shanghai for an important teacher-training conference — an occasion that aged me several years in the space of about three hours. The root of the disaster was embarrassingly simple: I'd checked the departure time wrong. My ticket said 9:40; some deeply confident part of my brain had filed it as 11:40. I discovered the truth at 7:15, staring at my phone with toothpaste still in my mouth. What followed was a masterpiece of haste. I threw on clothes that only technically matched, grabbed a bag I'd half-packed, and sprinted for the metro while attempting to book a taxi as a backup — with the focus and grace of a person being chased. The metro, naturally, was delayed. This is where the story turns: I made the snap decision to abandon it at a halfway station and take a taxi instead, and by pure dumb luck, one was dropping off right there. The driver, upon hearing 'airport, as fast as legally possible', turned out to be a man who took that phrase as a personal mission statement. I checked in with exactly nineteen minutes to spare, still adjusting my shirt, earning a look from the gate agent that could curdle milk. On the plane, heart finally slowing, I did the review: the real error wasn't misreading a time — people do that constantly. It was that I had no buffer. That near-disaster rebuilt my travel habits from the ground up: everything now leaves ninety minutes earlier than feels necessary, alarms are doubled, and tickets are confirmed three times. And I'll admit it — I've never missed a flight since. So yes, doing something in a hurry taught me that speed is no substitute for a margin, a lesson I paid for in adrenaline and learned for free in the end.
